messages.author: cd76564ddb5e3c29
messages.subject: spatiotemporal model validation and forecasting
parts:
Hi all, 

I am seeking after some help with model validation and forecasting from spatiotemporal models (this is my first attempt doing this using R-Inla, I am relatively new to INLA and still exploring it)

I have been trying to do these with some example data given in https://github.com/aritz-adin/Identifiability_Constraints_article/blob/main/R/CARmodels_INLA.R 
This is early data of Breast cancer mortality risk. So the model concerns estimating relative risk using Expected counts. 

My intention is to first validate the model using last 4 years data and forecast for next 2 years.  In the attached code I have prepared data frames for model validation (set NA for observed counts in last 4 years)  and forecasting (set NA for both observed and expected counts in the next 2 years). The model is Poison GLM with random effects Knorr-Held (2000) Type 4.

I am not sure about the followings and would appreciate some help: 
1. Do. the expected counts in the validation set also needs to be set as NA? 
2. The model for relative risk requires an expected count (E), but as the forecast dataset would not ideally have these, Eoes not including the E part in the inla() function makes sense? I mean is it really estimating relative risk if excluded? If not  how do I included expected counts in the forecast set? 
2. I would like to compute RMSE, MAE and Person correlation coefficient for the validation set. I understand that Model$summary.fitted.values give estimates  for the mean. But, how do I get estimates for the Observed values (i.e Y)? This is required to compute these discrepancy measures.

Many thanks for the help
Aminath

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatiotemporal model validation and forecasting
parts:
Sorry for not being clear.

In the model
 y ~ Poisson(rE)
where y and E are given to model r. Setting E=NA inla will treat it as E=1. And inla does the computations for the inference for r (mean, mode, quantiles, and the full distribution if you ask). Given r, E is used to get y, considering the equation r = y/E.

E is a function of population (and gender and age specific rates, usually). Therefore you need population forecasts to compute E for the forecasting of y (of course, you estimate r instead of rate). Once you have E and r, E _computed_ from the population and r _predicted_ (you can use summaries or even apply the full distribution estimated) by your model, you can apply the equation aforementioned.

best regards,
Elias
